claim: Modifications in the tRNA anticodon loop, adjacent to the three-nucleotide anticodon, influence translation fidelity by stabilizing the tRNA to allow for accurate reading of the mRNA genetic code.
source: Modifications in the tRNA anticodon loop, adjacent to the three-nucleotide anticodon, influence translation fidelity by stabilizing the tRNA to allow for accurate reading of the mRNA genetic code.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the subsequent structural and biochemical findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The N1-methylguanosine modification at guanine nucleotide 37 (m1G37) is located in the anticodon loop and immediately adjacent to the anticodon nucleotides 34, 35, 36.
source: One example is the N1-methylguanosine modification at guanine nucleotide 37 (m1G37) located in the anticodon loop andimmediately adjacent to the anticodon nucleotides 34, 35, 36.
evidence: This is a structural description confirmed by the crystal structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: The absence of m1G37 in tRNAPro causes +1 frameshifting on polynucleotide, slippery codons.
source: The absence of m1G37 in tRNAPro causes +1 frameshifting on polynucleotide, slippery codons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript and cited previous studies.

claim: Certain codon–anticodon contexts and the lack of m1G37 destabilize interactions of tRNAPro with the P site of the ribosome.
source: The structures reveal that certain codon–anticodon contexts and the lack of m1G37 destabilize interactions of tRNAPro with the P site of the ribosome, causing large conformational changes typically only seen during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the crystal structures presented in the manuscript showing different tRNA positions and conformational changes.

claim: Destabilization of tRNAPro in the P site causes large conformational changes typically only seen during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs.
source: The structures reveal that certain codon–anticodon contexts and the lack of m1G37 destabilize interactions of tRNAPro with the P site of the ribosome, causing large conformational changes typically only seen during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparisons with EF-G-containing translocation intermediate structures.

claim: Nucleotide 37 is adjacent to the anticodon and is modified in >70% of all tRNAs.
source: For example, nucleotide 37 is adjacent to the anticodon (Figure 1A) and is modified in >70% of all tRNAs (Machnicka et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Machnicka et al., 2014.

claim: The two most common modifications at nucleotide 37 are 6-threonylcarbamoyladenosine (t6A) and 1-methylguanosine (m1G), which together account for >60% of nucleotide 37 modifications.
source: The two most common modifications at nucleotide 37 are 6-threonylcarbamoyladenosine (t6A) and 1-methylguanosine (m1G), which together account for >60% of nucleotide 37 modifications (Boccaletto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Boccaletto et al., 2018.

claim: The t6A37 modification in tRNALys and the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro are thought to stabilize the tertiary structure of the anticodon loop for high-affinity binding to their cognate codons.
source: Both the t6A37 modification in tRNALys and the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro are thought to stabilize the tertiary structure of the anticodon loop for high-affinity binding to their cognate codons (Murphy et al., 2004; Sundaram et al., 2000; Nguyen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Murphy et al., 2004; Sundaram et al., 2000; Nguyen et al., 2019.

claim: The m1G37 modification prevents the ribosome from shifting out of the three-nucleotide mRNA codon frame ('frameshifting') to ensure the correct polypeptide is expressed.
source: The m1G37 modification also prevents the ribosome from shifting out of the three-nucleotide mRNA codon frame ('frameshifting') to ensure the correct polypeptide is expressed (Björk et al., 1989; Li et al., 1997; Urbonavicius et al., 2001; Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations: Björk et al., 1989; Li et al., 1997; Urbonavicius et al., 2001; Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: The m1G37 modification is present in >95% of all three tRNAPro isoacceptors across all three domains of life.
source: The m1G37 modification is present in >95% of all three tRNAPro isoacceptors across all three domains of life (Boccaletto et al., 2018; Björk et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boccaletto et al., 2018; Björk et al., 1989.

claim: The absence of m1G37 in tRNAPro causes high levels of +1 frameshifting on 'slippery' or polynucleotide mRNA sequences where four nucleotides encode for a single proline codon.
source: The absence of m1G37 in tRNAPro causes high levels of +1 frameshifting on so-called 'slippery' or polynucleotide mRNA sequences where four nucleotides encode for a single proline codon (Björk et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Björk et al., 1989.

claim: A +1 slippery codon for tRNAPro-CGG consists of the CCC proline codon and either an additional C or U to form a four-nucleotide codon, CCC-(U/C).
source: In the case of the tRNAPro-CGG isoacceptor (anticodon is shown 5'-3'), a +1 slippery codon consists of the CCC proline codon and either an additional C or U to form a four-nucleotide codon, CCC-(U/C) (Sroga et al., 1992; Qian et al., 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sroga et al., 1992; Qian et al., 1998.

claim: tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 results in the ribosome being unable to distinguish a correct from an incorrect codon–anticodon interaction during decoding at the aminoacyl (A) site.
source: tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 results in the ribosome being unable to distinguish a correct from an incorrect codon–anticodon interaction during decoding at the aminoacyl (A) site (Nguyen et al., 2019; Maehigashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nguyen et al., 2019; Maehigashi et al., 2014.

claim: The miscoding event in the A site does not cause the shift in the mRNA frame despite the tRNAPro-CGG anticodon stem-loop nucleotides becoming more mobile.
source: However, this miscoding event does not cause the shift in the mRNA frame in the A site despite the tRNAPro-CGG anticodon stem-loop nucleotides become more mobile (Maehigashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maehigashi et al., 2014.

claim: The absence of the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro causes a ~5% frameshifting frequency during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the A to the peptidyl (P) site.
source: The absence of the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro causes a ~ 5% frameshifting frequency during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the A to the peptidyl (P) site and a ~40% frameshifting frequency once the mRNA-tRNA pair has reached the P site.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analyses referenced in the text.

claim: The absence of the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro causes a ~40% frameshifting frequency once the mRNA-tRNA pair has reached the P site.
source: The absence of the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro causes a ~ 5% frameshifting frequency during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the A to the peptidyl (P) site and a ~40% frameshifting frequency once the mRNA-tRNA pair has reached the P site.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analyses referenced in the text.

claim: When tRNAPro-CGG lacks m1G37 and decodes a +1 slippery codon, both the process of translocation and the unique environment of the P site appear to contribute to the inability of the ribosome to maintain the mRNA frame.
source: When tRNAPro-CGG lacks m1G37 and decodes a +1 slippery codon, both the process of translocation and the unique environment of the P site appear to contribute to the inability of the ribosome to maintain the mRNA frame.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic and structural data presented.

claim: In circumstances where mRNA frameshifting is caused by changes in the tRNA such as the absence of modifications or changes in the size of the anticodon loop, the shift into the +1 frame is observed upon direct tRNA binding at the P site.
source: In circumstances where mRNA frameshifting is caused by changes in the tRNA such as the absence of modifications or changes in the size of the anticodon loop as found in frameshift suppressor tRNAs, primer extension assays demonstrated that the shift into the +1 frame is observed upon direct tRNA binding at the P site (Phelps et al., 2006; Walker and Fredrick, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Phelps et al., 2006; Walker and Fredrick, 2006.

claim: The presence of a nascent polypeptide chain, the acylation status of the tRNA, and the presence of a tRNA in the A site do not appear to contribute to the ability of frameshift-prone tRNAs to cause frameshifting.
source: Furthermore, the presence of a nascent polypeptide chain, the acylation status of the tRNA (deacylated or aminoacylated), and even the presence of a tRNA in the A site do not appear to contribute to the ability of these tRNAs to cause frameshifting.
evidence: This is based on primer extension assays referenced in the text.

claim: Frameshift suppressor tRNASufA6 contains an extra nucleotide in its anticodon loop and undergoes high levels of +1 frameshifting on slippery proline codons.
source: Frameshift suppressor tRNASufA6 contains an extra nucleotide in its anticodon loop and undergoes high levels of +1 frameshifting on slippery proline codons (Björk et al., 1989; Qian et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Björk et al., 1989; Qian et al., 1998.

claim: The structure of the anticodon stem-loop (ASL) of the tRNASufA6 bound directly at the P site revealed that its anticodon engages the slippery CCC-U proline codon in the +1 frame.
source: The structure of the anticodon stem-loop (ASL) of the tRNASufA6 bound directly at the P site revealed that its anticodon engages the slippery CCC-U proline codon in the +1 frame (Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hong et al., 2018.

claim: The full-length tRNASufA6 bound at the P site reveals that the small 30S subunit head domain swivels and tilts, a movement that is similar to the one that is caused by the GTPase elongation factor-G (EF-G) upon translocation of the tRNAs through the ribosome.
source: Further, the full-length tRNASufA6 bound at the P site reveals that the small 30S subunit head domain swivels and tilts, a movement that is similar to the one that is caused by the GTPase elongation factor-G (EF-G) upon translocation of the tRNAs through the ribosome that several groups have attempted to characterize (Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Wasserman et al., 2016; Belardinelli et al., 2016a, Nguyen and Whitford, 2016, Guo and Noller, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ermolenko and Noller, 2011; Wasserman et al., 2016; Belardinelli et al., 2016a, Nguyen and Whitford, 2016, Guo and Noller, 2012.

claim: The process of mRNA-tRNA translocation is coupled to 30S head domain swivel and tilting which is distinct from other conformational changes the ribosome undergoes including intersubunit rotation.
source: The process of mRNA-tRNA translocation is coupled to this head domain swivel and tilting which is distinct from other conformational changes the ribosome undergoes including intersubunit rotation (Wasserman et al., 2016; Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Holtkamp et al., 2014; Belardinelli et al., 2016b; Guo and Noller, 2012, Nguyen and Whitford, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wasserman et al., 2016; Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Holtkamp et al., 2014; Belardinelli et al., 2016b; Guo and Noller, 2012, Nguyen and Whitford, 2016.

claim: The 70S-tRNASufA6 structure shows head domain movement in the absence of EF-G, suggesting that a +1 frameshift event caused by frameshift-prone tRNAs dysregulates some aspect of translocation.
source: However, the 70S-tRNASufA6 structure is in the absence of EF-G, suggesting that a +1 frameshift event caused by frameshift-prone tRNAs dysregulates some aspect of translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: The structure of P-site ASLPro interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon was solved to a resolution of 3.1 Å.
source: The structure of P-site ASLPro interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon was solved to a resolution of 3.1 Å and reveals that the three nucleotides of the anticodon (nucleotides G36-G35-C34) form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 mRNA codon, respectively (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: In the structure of P-site ASLPro interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon, the three nucleotides of the anticodon (nucleotides G36-G35-C34) form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 mRNA codon.
source: The structure of P-site ASLPro interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon was solved to a resolution of 3.1 Å and reveals that the three nucleotides of the anticodon (nucleotides G36-G35-C34) form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 mRNA codon, respectively (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The anticodon of ASLPro interacts with the cognate CCG codon in the canonical or 0 mRNA frame.
source: The anticodon interacts with the codon in the canonical or 0 mRNA frame indicating a frameshift has not occurred.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The X-ray structure of ASLPro bound to a CCC-U codon was solved to a resolution of 3.4 Å.
source: In this X-ray structure solved to a resolution of 3.4 Å, we find two different conformations of the codon–anticodon interaction in the two molecules of the crystallographic asymmetric unit (Figure 1C and D and Table 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: In the structure of ASLPro bound to a CCC-U codon, two different conformations of the codon–anticodon interaction are found in the two molecules of the crystallographic asymmetric unit.
source: In this X-ray structure solved to a resolution of 3.4 Å, we find two different conformations of the codon–anticodon interaction in the two molecules of the crystallographic asymmetric unit (Figure 1C and D and Table 2 and Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: In the first ribosome molecule of the ASLPro-CCC-U structure, nucleotides G36 and G35 of ASLPro form Watson–Crick base-pairs with the first two nucleotides of the 0-frame mRNA codon.
source: In the first ribosome molecule, nucleotides G36 and G35 of ASLPro form Watson–Crick base-pairs with the first two nucleotides of the 0-frame mRNA codon (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A mismatch C+3•C34 forms at the third base-pair position of the codon–anticodon interaction in the first ribosome molecule of the ASLPro-CCC-U structure and contains a single hydrogen bond between the Watson–Crick face of C+3 (the N3 position) and C34 (the N4 position).
source: A mismatch C+3•C34 forms at the third base-pair position of the codon–anticodon interaction and contains a single hydrogen bond between the Watson–Crick face of C+3 (the N3 position) and C34 (the N4 position).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The distance between the anticodon nucleotide C34 and the mRNA nucleotide C+3 is increased in the P site as compared to this same mRNA-tRNA pair in the A site (3.6 Å vs. 3.1 Å).
source: The distance between the anticodon nucleotide C34 and the mRNA nucleotide C+3 is increased in the P site as compared to this same mRNA-tRNA pair in the A site (3.6 Å vs. 3.1 Å Maehigashi et al., 2014), indicating that the interaction has weakened.
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure (Maehigashi et al., 2014).

claim: In the other ribosome molecule in the crystallographic asymmetric unit of the ASLPro-CCC-U structure, the codon–anticodon interaction is in the +1 frame.
source: Strikingly, in the other ribosome molecule in the crystallographic asymmetric unit, the codon–anticodon interaction is in the +1 frame (Figure 1D and Video 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In the +1 frame conformation of the ASLPro-CCC-U structure, the first two nucleotides of the anticodon (G36-G35) form Watson–Crick base-pairs with C+2-C+3 nucleotides of the mRNA codon.
source: The first two nucleotides of the anticodon (G36-G35) form Watson–Crick base-pairs with C+2-C+3 nucleotides of the mRNA codon, respectively.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: In the +1 frame conformation of the ASLPro-CCC-U structure, the first nucleotide of the proline codon, C+1, no longer interacts with the tRNA and does not appear to make any interactions with the ribosome.
source: The first nucleotide of the proline codon, C+1, no longer interacts with the tRNA and does not appear to make any interactions with the ribosome.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: At the third position of the codon–anticodon interaction in the +1 frame, a cis-Watson–Crick U+4•C34 pair forms that contains a single hydrogen bond between the Watson–Crick face of U+4 (the O4 position) and C34 (the N4 position).
source: At the third position of the codon–anticodon interaction, a cis-Watson–Crick U+4•C34 pair forms that contains a single hydrogen bond between the Watson–Crick face of U+4 (the O4 position) and C34 (the N4 position) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Although the m1G37 modification is present in ASLPro, the shift in the +1 frame can still occur.
source: Therefore, although the m1G37 modification is present in ASLPro, the shift in the +1 frame can still occur.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of the +1 frame in the crystal structure with m1G37 present.

claim: The presence of a near-cognate, slippery codon is sufficient to promote a +1 mRNA frameshift.
source: These data indicate that the presence of a near-cognate, slippery codon is sufficient to promote a +1 mRNA frameshift.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data showing +1 frameshifting with m1G37 present.

claim: Biochemical studies of other near-cognate mRNA-tRNA pairs in the P site show frameshifting in both directions on the mRNA.
source: Consistent with our observations, biochemical studies of other near-cognate mRNA-tRNA pairs in the P site also show frameshifting in both directions on the mRNA (Zaher and Green, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zaher and Green, 2009.

claim: A structure of tRNAPro-CGG containing the m1G37 modification bound to a cognate CCG codon in the ribosomal P site was solved to a resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: As a control, we solved a structure of tRNAPro-CGG containing the m1G37 modification bound to a cognate CCG codon in the ribosomal P site to a resolution of 3.2 Å (Figure 2A and Table 3 and Video 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: tRNAPro-CGG containing m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon binds in the classical P/P state.
source: tRNAPro-CGG binds in the classical P/P state (bound to the P site on the 50S and the 30S subunits) and interacts with the proline codon in the 0 frame.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon, the G36-G35-C34 anticodon nucleotides form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 proline codon nucleotides.
source: Specifically, the G36-G35-C34 anticodon nucleotides form three Watson–Crick base-pairs with the C+1-C+2-G+3 proline codon nucleotides, respectively (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The methyl group at position 1 of the nucleobase of G37 stacks with the nucleobase of anticodon nucleotide G36 to form a canonical four-nucleotide stack between nucleotides 34–37.
source: The methyl group at position 1 of the nucleobase of G37 stacks with the nucleobase of anticodon nucleotide G36 to form a canonical four-nucleotide stack between nucleotides 34–37.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The anticodon stack is important for productive interactions with both mRNA and the ribosome.
source: This anticodon stack is important for productive interactions with both mRNA and the ribosome (Maehigashi et al., 2014; Grosjean et al., 1976; Gustilo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maehigashi et al., 2014; Grosjean et al., 1976; Gustilo et al., 2008.

claim: tRNAPro isoacceptors do not appear to spontaneously move into the +1 frame on non-slippery codons.
source: The P/P location of tRNAPro-CGG is thus consistent with functional assays demonstrating that tRNAPro isoacceptors do not appear to spontaneously move into the +1 frame on non-slippery codons (Björk et al., 1989; Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Björk et al., 1989; Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: A 3.9 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking the m1G37 modification (G37 Δm1) and interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon in the P site was solved.
source: We next solved a 3.9 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking the m1G37 modification (G37 Δm1) and interacting with a cognate CCG proline codon in the P site (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D and Table 3 and Video 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon adopts a P/P orientation.
source: Although the m1G37 modification was previously shown to be critical for high-affinity binding and decoding of the cognate CCG codon at the A site (Nguyen et al., 2019), its influence on the overall conformation of tRNAPro-CGG in the P site appears to be minimal as the tRNA adopts a P/P orientation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a cognate CCG codon, the mRNA remains in the 0 frame with three Watson–Crick base-pair interactions between the codon and the anticodon.
source: Notably, the mRNA remains in the 0 frame with three Watson–Crick base-pair interactions between the codon and the anticodon (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The absence of the m1G37 modification correlates with a slightly weaker U32-A38 pairing when compared to modified tRNAPro-CGG.
source: The absence of the m1G37 modification correlates with a slightly weaker U32-A38 pairing when compared to modified tRNAPro-CGG (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: tRNAPro-GGG lacking m1G37 on a non-slippery codon remained in the 0 frame according to toeprint analyses.
source: This observation is also consistent with toeprint analyses demonstrating that tRNAPro-GGG lacking m1G37 on a non-slippery codon remained in the 0 frame (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: A ribosome structure of tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a +1 slippery CCC-U codon in the P site was solved to a resolution of 3.2 Å.
source: In an attempt to reconcile the exact role of the m1G37 modification in tRNAPro-CGG in the context of a +1 slippery CCC-U codon, we next solved a ribosome structure of this complex in the P site to a resolution of 3.2 Å (Figure 2C and Table 3 and Video 2).
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: tRNAPro-CGG with m1G37 bound to a slippery CCC-U codon moves from the P site towards the E site, adopting a position referred to as e*/E.
source: Unexpectedly, tRNAPro-CGG moves from the P site towards the E site, adopting a position on the ribosome which we refer to as e*/E (Hong et al., 2018) (where e* signifies an intermediate position between the 30S subunit P and the E sites and E signifies a 50S E-site position) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The e*/E position of tRNAPro-CGG when bound to a slippery codon is different from the classical P/P position that the same tRNA adopts when it interacts with a cognate CCG codon.
source: The e*/E position of tRNAPro-CGG when bound to this slippery codon is different from the classical P/P position that the same tRNA adopts when it interacts with a cognate CCG codon (compare Figure 2A with Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed by comparing the crystal structures shown in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: The ability of tRNAPro-CGG to move towards the E site when bound to a slippery proline codon suggests that it is this near-cognate codon–anticodon interaction alone that is sufficient to destabilize tRNAPro-CGG.
source: Therefore, the ability of tRNAPro-CGG to move towards the E site when bound to a slippery proline codon suggests that it is this near-cognate codon–anticodon interaction alone that is sufficient to destabilize tRNAPro-CGG (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: The e*/E position of the tRNAPro-CGG-mRNA pair is coupled to large conformational changes of the 30S head domain.
source: The e*/E position of the tRNAPro-CGG-mRNA pair is additionally coupled to large conformational changes of the 30S head domain (Figure 3 and Video 2).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 30S head domain swivels in a ~18° counterclockwise direction while also undergoing a ~5° tilt away from the ribosome and perpendicular to the mRNA path in the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure.
source: The head domain swivels in a ~18° counterclockwise direction while also undergoing a ~5° tilt away from the ribosome and perpendicular to the mRNA path (Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014)
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure and compared to reference structures.

claim: The head domain is comprised of 16S rRNA nucleotides 930–1380 and seven ribosomal proteins (S3, S7, S9, S10, S13, S14, and S19).
source: The head domain is comprised of 16S rRNA nucleotides 930–1380 and seven ribosomal proteins (S3, S7, S9, S10, S13, S14, and S19) (Belardinelli et al., 2016a; Guo and Noller, 2012)
evidence: This is a structural definition supported by citations to Belardinelli et al., 2016a; Guo and Noller, 2012.

claim: The head domain moves as a rigid body during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs on the 30S.
source: The head domain is comprised of 16S rRNA nucleotides 930–1380 and seven ribosomal proteins (S3, S7, S9, S10, S13, S14, and S19) (Belardinelli et al., 2016a; Guo and Noller, 2012) that collectively move as a rigid body during EF-G-mediated translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pairs on the 30S (Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: The swivel and tilting of the head domain of e*/E tRNAPro-CGG occurs in the absence of EF-G.
source: The same swivel and tilting of the head domain of e*/E tRNAPro-CGG occurs but our structure lacks EF-G.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure which does not contain EF-G.

claim: Even with the m1G37 modification, interactions of tRNAPro-CGG with the P site are destabilized when bound to a near-cognate codon, promoting its movement toward the E site along with 30S head domain swivel and tilting.
source: This result indicates that even with the m1G37 modification, interactions of tRNAPro-CGG with the P site are destabilized when bound to a near-cognate codon, promoting its movement toward the E site along with 30S head domain swivel and tilting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: The ribosome interacts extensively with the mRNA in the A site to ensure accurate decoding but interacts less substantially with the P-site codon, while the E-site mRNA codon is the least monitored.
source: The ribosome interacts extensively with the mRNA in the A site to ensure accurate decoding but interacts less substantially with the P-site codon, while the E-site mRNA codon is the least monitored.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ribosome function.

claim: The ribosome interacts with E-site mRNA at two positions through non-sequence-specific contacts: 16S rRNA nucleotide G693 stacks with the first nucleotide of the E-site mRNA codon and the G926 nucleobase contacts the phosphate of the third mRNA codon nucleotide.
source: The ribosome interacts with E-site mRNA at two positions through non-sequence-specific contacts: 16S rRNA nucleotide G693 stacks with the first nucleotide of the E-site mRNA codon and the G926 nucleobase contacts the phosphate of the third mRNA codon nucleotide (Figure 4B and C; Selmer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Selmer et al., 2006 and shown in Figures 4B and C.

claim: The e* position of tRNAPro-CGG signifies that the tRNA is closer to the E site than the P site on the 30S.
source: The e* position of tRNAPro-CGG signifies that the tRNA is closer to the E site than the P site on the 30S, however it is similar to the pe/E tRNA position seen in translocation intermediate ribosome structures containing EF-G (Figure 4D; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison with translocation intermediate structures.

claim: Only two nucleotides of the codon–anticodon interaction of the pe/E tRNA are positioned in the E site leaving a pocket for an additional nucleotide to occupy upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair.
source: Only two nucleotides of the codon–anticodon interaction of the pe/E tRNA are positioned in the E site leaving a pocket for an additional nucleotide to occupy upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair (Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014) (compare Figure 4C with Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the structure containing an e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a near-cognate, slippery codon, the first three nucleotides of the codon fully occupy the E site.
source: In our structure containing an e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a near-cognate, slippery codon, the first three nucleotides of the codon fully occupy the E site (Figure 4E), despite the codon–anticodon adopting an intermediate position on the 30S between the P and the E sites.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The compaction of the mRNA in the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure means there is no space for the entire four-nucleotide codon in the E site upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair.
source: This compaction of the mRNA means there is no space for the entire four-nucleotide codon in the E site upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: The mRNA path 5' from the E site turns sharply by ~100° as the mRNA transits to the outside of the ribosome.
source: Additionally, the mRNA path 5' from the E site turns sharply by ~100° as the mRNA transits to the outside of the ribosome (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Upon full translocation of the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG to the E site, the first nucleotide of the codon would be displaced from the E site to accommodate the three-nucleotide codon or the last three nucleotides of the CCC-U codon, positioning the mRNA in the +1 frame.
source: In the case of e*/E tRNAPro-CGG, upon full translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair to the E site, the first nucleotide of the codon would be displaced from the E site to accommodate the three-nucleotide codon or the last three nucleotides of the CCC-U codon. This placement would position the mRNA in the +1 frame.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation and the constraints of the E site.

claim: The ribosome minimally interacts with the mRNA-tRNA pair in the P site: 16S rRNA C1400 contacts G966 and stacks with the third base-pair of the codon–anticodon.
source: The ribosome minimally interacts with the mRNA-tRNA pair in the P site: 16S rRNA C1400 contacts G966 and stacks with the third base-pair of the codon–anticodon (Figure 5A; Selmer et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Selmer et al., 2006 and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The G966-C1400 pair remains intact during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the P to the E site as part of the head domain.
source: The G966-C1400 pair remains intact during translocation of the mRNA-tRNA pair from the P to the E site as part of the head domain, as evidenced by ribosome structures in translocation intermediate states containing EF-G (Figure 5B). (Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the structure containing e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a CCC-U codon, the G966-C1400 interaction is ablated.
source: In our structure containing e*/E tRNAPro-CGG bound to a CCC-U codon, the G966-C1400 interaction is ablated (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The disruption of the G966-C1400 interaction can be attributed to a dysregulation caused by the spontaneous translocation event.
source: Since the G966-C1400 interaction is effectively the bridge between the head and body domains, this disruption can be attributed to a dysregulation caused by this spontaneous translocation event.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observation.

claim: A 4.1 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37(Δm1) and interacting with a near-cognate, slippery CCC-U codon at the P site was solved.
source: Finally, we solved a 4.1 Å structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37(Δm1) and interacting with a near-cognate, slippery CCC-U codon at the P site.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a CCC-U codon, the electron density for the majority of the tRNAPro-CGG on the 50S subunit is well-resolved, indicating that the tRNA has moved towards the E site on the 50S subunit.
source: The electron density for the majority of the tRNAPro-CGG on the 50S subunit is well-resolved, indicating that, similar to the analogous structure solved in the presence of the m1G37 modification (Figure 2C), the tRNA has also moved towards the E site on the 50S subunit (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a CCC-U codon, the electron density is weak for the tRNAPro-CGG ASL and E-site mRNA indicating these regions are dynamic.
source: In contrast, the electron density is weak for the tRNAPro-CGG ASL and E-site mRNA indicating these regions are dynamic in the context of slippery codon and in the absence of m1G37 modification (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Disordering of tRNAPro G37(Δm1) starts approximately at the beginning of the anticodon loop at nucleotides U32-A38.
source: Disordering of tRNAPro G37(Δm1) starts approximately at the beginning of the anticodon loop at nucleotides U32-A38.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure.

claim: In the structure of tRNAPro-CGG lacking m1G37 bound to a CCC-U codon, the 30S head domain region is disordered.
source: Correspondingly, the 30S head domain region is also disordered (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D), whereas the only region of the 30S body domain with poor electron density is the P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In the mRNA-tRNA pairing that causes high levels of frameshifting (tRNAPro lacking m1G37 on CCC-U codon), interactions with the tRNA are destabilized in the P site resulting in the codon–anticodon adopting an e* location and high mobility of the 30S head domain.
source: Taken together, in this mRNA-tRNA pairing that causes high levels of frameshifting, interactions with the tRNA are destabilized in the P site resulting in the codon–anticodon adopting an e* location and high mobility of the 30S head domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The m1G37 modification in tRNAPro-CGG influences the overall stability of tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome and causes large conformational changes between the tRNA and the 30S head domain.
source: We find that this single methyl group influences the overall stability of tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome in an unexpected manner and causes large conformational changes between the tRNA and the 30S head domain, a domain known to move extensively during translocation of the tRNAs (Wasserman et al., 2016; Ratje et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the structural data presented.

claim: The methylation of m1G37 alone does not stabilize tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome; instead, its position is heavily influenced by interactions with a slippery proline codon.
source: However, the methylation alone does not stabilize tRNAPro-CGG on the ribosome and, instead, its position is heavily influenced by interactions with a slippery proline codon.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the structural data presented.

claim: The location on the ribosome where frameshifting can occur is likely dependent on the type of frameshift (in the positive or negative direction on the mRNA) and whether tRNA or mRNA causes the frameshift.
source: The location on the ribosome where frameshifting can occur is likely dependent on the type of frameshift (in the positive or negative directionon the mRNA) and whether tRNA or mRNA causes the frameshift (Dinman, 2012; Dunkle and Dunham, 2015; Atkins et al., 2016; Korniy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dinman, 2012; Dunkle and Dunham, 2015; Atkins et al., 2016; Korniy et al., 2019.

claim: The codon–anticodon interaction located in the 30S A site is strictly monitored by conserved 16S rRNA nucleotides to select for cognate tRNA.
source: While the codon–anticodon interaction located in the 30S A site is strictly monitored by conserved 16S rRNA nucleotides to select for cognate tRNA (Ogle et al., 2002), there are comparatively few interactions with the codon–anticodon when positioned within the P and E sites, underscoring their different functional roles during the translation cycle.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogle et al., 2002.

claim: There are comparatively few interactions with the codon–anticodon when positioned within the P and E sites.
source: While the codon–anticodon interaction located in the 30S A site is strictly monitored by conserved 16S rRNA nucleotides to select for cognate tRNA (Ogle et al., 2002), there are comparatively few interactions with the codon–anticodon when positioned within the P and E sites, underscoring their different functional roles during the translation cycle.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ribosome function.

claim: The relative absence of interactions in the P and E sites provides an opportunity for the mRNA to shift out of frame.
source: The relative absence of interactions in the P and E sites provides an opportunity for the mRNA to shift out of frame.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Some tRNAPro isoacceptors frameshift either during translocation from the A to the P site or after the translocation step and once positioned in the P site.
source: Some tRNAPro isoacceptors frameshift either during translocation from the A to the P site or after the translocation step and once positioned in the P site (Gamper et al., 2015a; Gamper et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gamper et al., 2015a; Gamper et al., 2015b.

claim: Interactions with the P-site tRNA are limited to only 16S rRNA P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339 with the anticodon stem and 16S rRNA C1400 with the anticodon nucleotide 34.
source: This frameshift is likely possible because interactions with the P-site tRNA are limited to only 16S rRNA P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339 with the anticodon stem and 16S rRNA C1400 with the anticodon nucleotide 34 (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The P/E loop appears to indirectly enforce the mRNA frame by gripping the P-site tRNA.
source: The P/E loop appears to indirectly enforce the mRNA frame by gripping the P-site tRNA and these interactions are maintained as the tRNA moves from the P site to a hybrid P/E state (Dunkle et al., 2011) and to a translocation intermediate pe/E state (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations and supported by citations to Dunkle et al., 2011 and Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: In the structures of ASLPro interacting with the mRNA in the 0 frame, there is well-resolved density for G1338 and A1339.
source: In the structures of ASLPro interacting with the mRNA in the 0 frame, there is well-resolved density for G1338 and A1339 (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D, G), while there is some disordering of these nucleotides in the context of ASLPro bound to the near-cognate, slippery codon in the +1 frame (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, F and I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures.

claim: There is some disordering of G1338 and A1339 in the context of ASLPro bound to the near-cognate, slippery codon in the +1 frame.
source: In the structures of ASLPro interacting with the mRNA in the 0 frame, there is well-resolved density for G1338 and A1339 (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,D, G), while there is some disordering of these nucleotides in the context of ASLPro bound to the near-cognate, slippery codon in the +1 frame (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, F and I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures.

claim: The inability for G1338 and A1339 to grip the anticodon stem when the codon–anticodon is in the +1 frame likely results in the destabilization of full-length tRNAPro in frameshift-competent contexts.
source: The inability for G1338 and A1339 to grip the anticodon stem when the codon–anticodon is in the +1 frame likely results in the destabilization of full-length tRNAPro in these frameshift-competent contexts (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Simulations of the ribosome undergoing large movements of the head domain during translocation implicate nucleotides G1338 and A1339 in the coupling of 30S head dynamics and displacement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site.
source: Simulations of the ribosome undergoing large movements of the head domain during translocation implicate nucleotides G1338 and A1339 in the coupling of 30S head dynamics and displacement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site (Nguyen and Whitford, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nguyen and Whitford, 2016.

claim: The lack of gripping by the P/E loop in the P site when a destabilized mRNA-tRNA interaction is present appears to bias tRNAPro toward the E site which, in turn, causes the 30S head domain to swivel and tilt as if EF-G were bound.
source: Therefore, the lack of gripping by the P/E loop in the P site when a destabilized mRNA-tRNA interaction is present, appears to bias tRNAPro toward the E site which, in turn, causes the 30S head domain to swivel and tilt as if EF-G were bound.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: 16S rRNA nucleotide G966 stacks with nucleotide 34 of the P-site tRNA anticodon.
source: In addition to P/E loop nucleotides G1338 and A1339, 16S rRNA nucleotide G966 is also part of the 30S head domain and stacks with nucleotide 34 of the P-site tRNA anticodon (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The 30S head is connected to the body domain via interactions of G966 with nucleotide C1400.
source: The 30S head is connected to the body domain via interactions of G966 with nucleotide C1400; the G966-C1400 pair remains stacked beneath the P-site tRNA and follows the tRNA as it moves to a hybrid P/E state and to a translocation pe/E intermediate state upon EF-G binding (Figure 5B; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Dunkle et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014; Dunkle et al., 2011 and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the case of P-site ASLPro interacting with a +1 slippery codon in the 0 or +1 frame, cis-Watson–Crick interactions form between C+3•C34 and U+4•C34, respectively.
source: In the case of P-site ASLPro interacting with a +1 slippery codon in the 0 or +1 frame, cis-Watson–Crick interactions form between C+3•C34 and U+4•C34, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: Both the C+3•C34 and U+4•C34 interactions appear to result in reduced stacking with C1400.
source: Both the C+3•C34 and U+4•C34 interactions appear to result in reduced stacking with C1400.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: In structures of full-length tRNAPro-mRNA pairs that cause +1 frameshifting and destabilization at the P site, the G966-C1400 interaction is broken.
source: In structures of full-length tRNAPro-mRNA pairs that cause +1 frameshifting and destabilization at the P site, the G966-C1400 interaction is broken (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The reduced interactions of G1338-A1339 and G966-C1400 with the tRNA appear to influence the movement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site.
source: Together, these results suggest a connection between the reduced interactions of G1338-A1339 and G966-C1400 with the tRNA that appear to influence the movement of the P-site tRNA towards the E site.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Substitution of G966 substantially reduces ribosome activity to ~10% despite the mutation not being lethal.
source: 16S rRNA nucleotides in the P site are generally more tolerable of mutations than the A-site 16S rRNA, although substitution of G966 substantially reduces ribosome activity to ~10% despite the mutation not being lethal (Abdi and Fredrick, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abdi and Fredrick, 2005.

claim: The G966 mutant is suppressed by a G1338A mutation, indicating that the G1338A mutation can stabilize interactions with the P-site tRNA even in the absence of the C1400-G966 interaction.
source: This G966 mutant is suppressed by a G1338A mutation, indicating that the G1338A mutation can stabilize interactions with the P-site tRNA even in the absence of the C1400-G966 interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on genetic suppression data.

claim: In the context of full-length mRNA-tRNA pairs that cause +1 frameshifting, both the tRNA and mRNA move from the P site to occupy a position between the E and the P site.
source: In the context of full-length mRNA-tRNA pairs that cause +1 frameshifting, both the tRNA and mRNA move from the P site to occupy a position between the E and the P site (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structures shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: The mRNA-tRNA placement in the e*/E tRNAPro structure is similar to the translocation intermediate containing EF-G.
source: This mRNA-tRNA placement is similar to the translocation intermediate containing EF-G (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previously published structure (Zhou et al., 2013).

claim: In the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure, e*/E tRNAPro is positioned slightly further away from the mRNA as compared to the EF-G containing structures containing a pe/tRNA.
source: In the structure presented here containing an e*/E tRNAPro as compared to the EF-G containing structures containing an pe/tRNA, e*/E tRNAPro is positioned slightly further away from the mRNA.
evidence: This is a comparison with EF-G-containing translocation intermediate structures.

claim: In the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure, the first position of the codon–anticodon forms a Watson–Crick interaction but the second and third nucleotides of the codon–anticodon are not within hydrogen bonding distances.
source: In the e*/E tRNAPro-CGG structure, the first position of the codon–anticodon forms a Watson–Crick interaction but the second and third nucleotides of the codon–anticodon are not within hydrogen bonding distances (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the EF-G-bound translocation intermediate structures, the codon–anticodon is not within bonding distance.
source: Interestingly, in the EF-G-bound translocation intermediate structures, the codon–anticodon is also not within bonding distance (Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2013.

claim: It is the disruptive nature of moving between tRNA binding sites that perturbs the interactions between the codon and anticodon and these interactions likely reform once the transition to the next tRNA binding site is complete.
source: These results suggest that it is the disruptive nature of moving between tRNA binding sites that perturbs the interactions between the codon and anticodon and these interactions likely reform once the transition to the next tRNA binding site is complete.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Upon EF-G binding, the head domain is predicted to first tilt and then swivel in a counterclockwise manner to translocate the two tRNAs to final E/E and P/P positions.
source: Upon EF-G binding, the head domain is predicted to first tilt and then swivel in a counterclockwise manner (as viewed with the E, P, A tRNA sites from left to right shown in Figure 2) to translocate the two tRNAs to final E/E and P/P positions (Wasserman et al., 2016; Nguyen and Whitford, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wasserman et al., 2016; Nguyen and Whitford, 2016.

claim: The departure of EF-G and reverse tilting of the head back towards the intersubunit space is followed by clockwise swivel, the rate-limiting step for translocation.
source: The departure of EF-G and reverse tilting of the head back towards the intersubunit space is followed by clockwise swivel, the rate-limiting step for translocation (Wasserman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wasserman et al., 2016.

claim: Frameshift-prone tRNAs cause spontaneous head swiveling and tilting once the tRNA occupies the P site after the mRNA frameshift has occurred.
source: Frameshift-prone tRNAs, such as tRNAPro-CGG, cause spontaneous head swiveling and tilting once the tRNA occupies the P site after the mRNA frameshift has occurred.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The inability of the ribosome to hold the P-site tRNA is influenced by weakening of the interactions of the P/E loop with the anticodon stem and by disruption of the C1400-G966 interaction.
source: The inability of the ribosome to hold the P-site tRNA is influenced by weakening of the interactions of the P/E loop with the anticodon stem and by disruption of the C1400-G966 interaction, both events likely major contributors to the dysregulation of the 30S head domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: The head domain is unable to maintain extensive interactions with the P-site tRNA and this failure leads to spontaneous translocation.
source: In other words, the head domain is unable to maintain extensive interactions with the P-site tRNA and this failure leads to spontaneous translocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Single molecule FRET (smFRET) studies of translocation events show that upon tRNA movement from the P to the E site, there is increased dissociation of the tRNA from the ribosome, bypassing the post-translocation E/E state.
source: Single molecule FRET (smFRET) studies of translocation events also show that upon tRNA movement from the P to the E site, there is increased dissociation of the tRNA from the ribosome, bypassing the post-translocation E/E state (Wasserman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wasserman et al., 2016.

claim: Once EF-G fully translocates tRNAPro-CGG to the post E/E state, there may be a further decrease in interactions between the tRNA and ribosome.
source: Consistent with these observations, we would expect that once EF-G fully translocates tRNAPro-CGG to the post E/E state, there may be a further decrease in interactions between the tRNA and ribosome.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations and smFRET data.

claim: The 30S head swivel and tilt movement in the absence of EF-G would likely prevent EF-G from binding until the head resets to a non-rotated state.
source: Additionally, our structures show 30S head swiveling and tilting in the absence of EF-G, concurrent with the +1 frameshift event. This 30S head swivel and tilt movement would likely prevent EF-G from binding until the the head resets to a non-rotated state.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations.

claim: EF-G residues located in the tip of domain IV interact with the anticodon stem-loop of the A-site tRNA during translocation to the P site.
source: EF-G residues located in the tip of domain IV interact with the anticodon stem-loop of the A-site tRNA during translocation to the P site (Zhou et al., 2013) and mutations in this domain slow the rate of translocation (Rodnina et al., 1997; Savelsbergh et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Rodnina et al., 1997; Savelsbergh et al., 2000.

claim: Mutations in EF-G domain IV slow the rate of translocation.
source: EF-G residues located in the tip of domain IV interact with the anticodon stem-loop of the A-site tRNA during translocation to the P site (Zhou et al., 2013) and mutations in this domain slow the rate of translocation (Rodnina et al., 1997; Savelsbergh et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rodnina et al., 1997; Savelsbergh et al., 2000.

claim: EF-G can restrict frameshifting and helps to maintain the mRNA frame on slippery codon sequences where spontaneous frameshifting occurs.
source: Recent studies using slippery codon sequences where spontaneous frameshifting occurs, EF-G can restrict frameshifting and helps to maintain the mRNA frame (Peng et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Peng et al., 2019.

claim: EF-G may have a role in mRNA frame maintenance in addition to its established function in translocation.
source: It is therefore an enticing hypothesis that EF-G may have a role in mRNA frame maintenance in addition to its established function in translocation.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations and recent studies.

claim: All three prokaryotic tRNAPro isoacceptors have the capacity to frameshift.
source: Although all three prokaryotic tRNAPro isoacceptors have the capacity to frameshift, whether they use similar mechanisms of action is unknown (Björk et al., 1989; Gamper et al., 2015a; Qian et al., 1998; O'Connor, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Björk et al., 1989; Gamper et al., 2015a; Qian et al., 1998; O'Connor, 2002.

claim: The m1G37 modification minimally influences frameshifting in proline isoacceptor tRNAPro-GGG (proL) in contrast to tRNAPro-cmo5UGG (proM).
source: The m1G37 modification minimally influences frameshifting in proline isoacceptor tRNAPro-GGG (proL) in contrast to tRNAPro-cmo5UGG (proM) (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: EF-P binds at the E site to overcome ribosome stalling induced by poly-proline codons.
source: EF-P binds at the E site to overcome ribosome stalling induced by poly-proline codons (Ude et al., 2013; Huter et al., 2017) and is critical in suppressing frameshifts on poly-proline stretches (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ude et al., 2013; Huter et al., 2017; Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: EF-P is critical in suppressing frameshifts on poly-proline stretches.
source: EF-P binds at the E site to overcome ribosome stalling induced by poly-proline codons (Ude et al., 2013; Huter et al., 2017) and is critical in suppressing frameshifts on poly-proline stretches (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: EF-P reduces +1 frameshifts with tRNAPro-GGG G37(Δm1) to an equivalent frequency as native tRNAPro-GGG.
source: While EF-P reduces +1 frameshifts with tRNAPro-GGG G37(Δm1) to an equivalent frequency as native tRNAPro-GGG, the absence or presence of m1G37 has little influence on the ability of isoacceptor tRNAPro-cmo5UGG to frameshift (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: The absence or presence of m1G37 has little influence on the ability of isoacceptor tRNAPro-cmo5UGG to frameshift.
source: While EF-P reduces +1 frameshifts with tRNAPro-GGG G37(Δm1) to an equivalent frequency as native tRNAPro-GGG, the absence or presence of m1G37 has little influence on the ability of isoacceptor tRNAPro-cmo5UGG to frameshift (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015a.

claim: Mechanistic differences between tRNAPro isoacceptors may be due to a combination of the codon–anticodon pairings on slippery codons and/or the influence of other modifications such as the cmo5U34 modification in tRNAPro-cmo5UGG.
source: These mechanistic differences may be due to a combination of the codon–anticodon pairings on slippery codons (tRNAPro-cmo5UGG and tRNAPro-GGG are cognate with slippery codons while tRNAPro-CGG is near-cognate [Nasvall et al., 2004]) and/or the influence of other modifications such as the cmo5U34 modification in tRNAPro-cmo5UGG (Masuda et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations and cited studies.

claim: tRNAPro-cmo5UGG and tRNAPro-GGG are cognate with slippery codons while tRNAPro-CGG is near-cognate.
source: These mechanistic differences may be due to a combination of the codon–anticodon pairings on slippery codons (tRNAPro-cmo5UGG and tRNAPro-GGG are cognate with slippery codons while tRNAPro-CGG is near-cognate [Nasvall et al., 2004]) and/or the influence of other modifications such as the cmo5U34 modification in tRNAPro-cmo5UGG (Masuda et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nasvall et al., 2004.

claim: tRNAPro-UGG lacking all modifications exhibits higher levels of frameshifting as compared to tRNAPro-UGG lacking only the m1G37 modification.
source: The possible synergistic effects of cmo5U34 and m1G37 in tRNAPro-cmo5UGG in preventing frameshifts is unclear, but tRNAPro-UGG lacking all modifications exhibits higher levels of frameshifting as compared to tRNAPro-UGG lacking only the m1G37 modification (Gamper et al., 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gamper et al., 2015b.

claim: If the presence of m1G37 in tRNAPro-cmo5UGG restricts its movement to the e*/E position, this tRNA isoacceptor may no longer be an optimal substrate for EF-P.
source: Since the presence of m1G37 in tRNAPro-cmo5UGG may restrict its movement to the e*/E position, this tRNA isoaccepor may no longer be an optimal substrate for EF-P, which is consistent with kinetic analyses (Gamper et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural observations and kinetic analyses.

claim: Chemically synthesized ASL was used to ensure complete m1G modification at position 37.
source: We used a chemically synthesized ASL to ensure complete m1G modification at position 37, as previously used to examine interactions in the A site (Maehigashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation to Maehigashi et al., 2014.

claim: Purification of Thermus thermophilus 70S ribosomes was performed as previously described.
source: Purification of Thermus thermophilus 70S ribosomes was performed as previously described (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.
